case_study_insert.main_stem: Copper Kettle Bakery (CKB) is a sole trader business in the artisan baking sector, employing a workforce of 12. Founded in 2011 by Rosa Jiménez, the bakery supplies wholesale pies, pastries and breads to 34 cafés across the city region, and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CKB plans to invest $145,000 in a new wholesale pie and pastry line, financed by a $70,000 five-year bank loan and $75,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $90,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.75 a unit and a selling price of $8.50, and currently produces 34,000 units a year. CKB faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 22% among weekend staff and its delivery van fleet is ageing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — September 2026: The bakery produced 2,150 wholesale boxes last month, with a defect rate of 2.9%, down from 4.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 12 to 7 per month. Average order fulfilment is 1.5 days. Flour and butter waste fell to 6.1% of input weight. A survey of 180 café owners found that 68% want same-day delivery, and 44% would pay up to $0.50 more per box for organic flour. 9 of 12 staff have completed on-the-job training on the new laminated-pastry process; the remaining 3 need off-the-job courses at the bakery college costing $600 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Copper Kettle Bakery as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has cut the base interest rate from 5.0% to 4.5% to support small businesses expanding their premises. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.00 to $12.72 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Wheat flour and butter costs have risen 13.5% year-on-year, bakery-price inflation is running at 7.8%, while consumer spending on artisan bakery goods grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: CKB plans to invest $145,000 in a wholesale pie and pastry line rather than opening a second retail shop. Explain two advantages for CKB of the wholesale expansion rather than the second shop.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The wholesale line leverages CKB's existing production capability and reputation with its 34 café customers, multiplying sales without the overheads of a second retail shop — lease deposits, refurbishment, shopfitting, till equipment and two extra retail staff. CKB can reach more outlets from one kitchen, spreading its $90,000 fixed costs across more units and pushing annual output toward the new line's potential while protecting the $4.75 variable cost through bulk flour and butter purchasing.

Point 2: Wholesale revenue is recurring and predictable: café owners reorder weekly boxes, smoothing cash flow against a $70,000 five-year bank loan and letting CKB plan production and van routes efficiently. A second retail shop would add location risk — footfall, parking, local competition — before loyalty is proven, whereas the wholesale trade is already validated by 68% of 180 surveyed café owners wanting same-day delivery. The wholesale route also compounds CKB's artisan brand story across the city region and keeps Rosa Jiménez's flat, autocratic structure workable, since one production lead can manage the line without diluting the personal oversight that defines a sole trader's quality guarantee.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Copper Kettle Bakery, its café customer base and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CKB is launching its wholesale pie and pastry range to new cafés. Consider a local radio sponsorship, a food-festival stall with free tastings, or a printed catalogue with introductory discounts. Which should CKB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio sponsorship: A weekly morning-show sponsorship around artisan breakfast time would reach city-region listeners, many of whom are café customers, and is far cheaper than television. It builds broad local awareness of the launch. Its weakness is that radio is a passive, audio-only medium — listeners cannot taste the pastry — and the audience includes many people outside the 34-café trade area, so wastage is significant for a 12-person sole trader whose marketing capacity and budget are limited by the $70,000 loan commitment.

Food-festival stall with free tastings: A stall at the city food festival puts the pies and pastries directly into the mouths of café owners and their customers, generating instant feedback, trial orders and word-of-mouth in exactly the target segment. Sampling converts sceptics quickly and photographs well for social media. The drawback is a one-off spike of attention with no guarantee of repeat wholesale orders after the festival ends, and the labour cost of manning the stall falls on the same 12-person team already stretched by weekend shifts.

Printed catalogue with introductory discounts: A professional catalogue mailed to the 180 surveyed café owners (44% of whom would pay up to $0.50 more per box for organic flour) directly drives wholesale enquiries, showcases the full new line with prices, and the introductory discount de-risks the first order. Catalogues can sit on café counters for weeks as a reminder. However, print reaches only existing prospects, conversion is slow and unmeasurable without follow-up calls, and printing and postage costs bite if response is below roughly 20%.

Recommendation: CKB should choose the printed catalogue with introductory discounts, supported by one food-festival tasting at launch rather than a full stall programme. The catalogue is the only option that reaches all 180 respondent cafés directly at low cost, matches the data-driven segmentation already in the operations log, and pushes the 68% wanting same-day delivery to try the line; it is rejected only as a stand-alone tool. Radio is rejected as untargeted and unmeasurable for a $70,000-loan-financed sole trader; the festival stall alone is rejected as a one-off spike that cannot sustain the weekly reorder volume the new line needs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CKB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CKB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the radio sponsorship and stand-alone festival stall are rejected.

questions.question_text: CKB's labour turnover has reached 22% among weekend staff. Explain two problems for CKB of this labour turnover.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: High weekend labour turnover means CKB constantly loses trained hands on its busiest days, forcing Rosa Jiménez to re-recruit and re-train weekend bakers repeatedly. Each leaver takes tacit knowledge of the laminated-pastry process, so defect rates edge upward (they are already 2.9%), rework and flour waste rise above the 6.1% benchmark, and the bakery misses the same-day delivery expectations of the 68% of café owners who want it — risking lost wholesale accounts worth far more than the cost of a weekend wage.

Point 2: Constant recruitment drives up costs and management strain for a sole trader: advertising, interview time, induction, uniforms and supervision all consume Rosa's hours that should go into production planning and the new $145,000 wholesale line. Instability also unsettles the 12 remaining employees, some of whom cover gaps unpaid, deepening the morale problem that caused 22% turnover in the first place. If it persists, CKB's flat autocratic structure loses credibility with weekend staff, service reliability to the 34 cafés suffers, and the fixed-cost absorption from 34,000 units of annual output slips, weakening the case for the expansion loan repayments.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid problem identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CKB's weekend operations, quality figures and expansion plan.

questions.question_text: CKB must train its remaining 3 staff on the new laminated-pastry process. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the bakery college. Which should CKB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training inside the bakery is directly relevant to CKB's own ovens, flour suppliers and pastry techniques, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 3 staff producing boxes during the busiest laminated-pastry season. Mistakes are made on real orders where feedback is immediate, and Rosa can coach flaws out of the process in person — critical for a sole trader who knows every batch. Drawbacks: if Rosa teaches while producing, her own output falls, bad habits can be passed on uncorrected, and there is no formal certification, which matters if café auditors or insurers ask for documented competency on the new line.

Off-the-job training: The bakery college course at $600 per employee — $1,800 for 3 staff — gives structured, up-to-date tuition, a recognised certificate and exposure to techniques beyond Rosa's own kitchen, such as waste reduction toward the 6.1% benchmark and food-safety hygiene. Time away from the bakery removes 3 staff for the course duration, however, pressuring weekend cover that is already failing at 22% turnover, and content is generic rather than CKB-specific, so fine-tuning on return would still be needed.

Decision: CKB should choose on-the-job training with a short college visit for certification only, rather than full off-the-job courses. It is nearly free, preserves weekend capacity CKB cannot spare, and matches the urgent need to stabilise the new line while the $70,000 loan is serviced. Full off-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because removing 25% of the workforce (3 of 12) from production during launch would strain same-day delivery promises and Rosa's supervision load; the $1,800 fee is affordable, but the output loss and generic content make it a poor substitute — though retaining a college certificate as a weekend-staff retention incentive is worth doing once the line stabilises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of on-the-job and off-the-job training with limited application to CKB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training options in the context of CKB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training options in the context of CKB with a well-justified decision explaining why full off-the-job training is rejected as the primary route.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CKB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $90,000 ÷ ($8.50 − $4.75) = $90,000 ÷ $3.75 = 24,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 24,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $8.50 − $4.75 = $3.75. Answer: contribution per unit is $3.75.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CKB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. CKB can compare the 24,000-unit break-even output with current production of 34,000 units to confirm a comfortable margin of safety of 10,000 units, informing Rosa whether the new pie and pastry line can absorb seasonal café demand dips without breaching the loan covenant.
2. The contribution per unit of $3.75 lets CKB model introductory launch discounts: a $0.50 cut to $8.00 would reduce contribution to $3.25, so Rosa can test whether the 44% of cafés willing to pay $0.50 extra for organic flour is a better margin lever than a promotional price.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $90,000 and the 24,000-unit break-even lets Rosa set minimum weekly café order quantities before dispatching vans, keeping each route profitable and protecting the $70,000 bank loan repayment schedule.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost (average total cost = $90,000 ÷ 34,000 units + $4.75 = $7.40 a unit) quarter by quarter, attack the 6.1% flour and butter waste with better batch sizing, and renegotiate the $4.75 variable cost with suppliers in the face of the 13.5% wheat and butter inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 24,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $8.50 − $4.75 = $3.75, and $90,000 ÷ $3.75 = 24,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.75. This is what each wholesale box of pies, pastries and breads contributes toward covering fixed costs after flour, butter and packaging are paid. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, Rosa can compare current output of 34,000 units with the 24,000-unit break-even to confirm a margin of safety of 10,000 units, reassuring herself and her bank that the wholesale line can absorb seasonal café dips without breaching the $70,000 loan schedule. Second, the $3.75 contribution lets Rosa test launch incentives: a $0.50 introductory cut would leave $3.25 per unit, so she knows any introductory offer needs volumes above roughly 27,700 units to keep the business beyond break-even for the year. Third, knowing the 24,000-unit break-even lets Rosa set minimum weekly café orders and van route density, ensuring every dispatched route recovers its fuel, the 6.1% flour and butter waste and its labour before the schedule is committed. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($90,000 ÷ 34,000 units + $4.75 = $7.40 a unit) gives Rosa a yardstick for the 2.9% defect rate: she can trace rework cost per box, decide whether the 44% of cafés wanting organic flour justify a price premium, and renegotiate the $4.75 variable cost with suppliers amid the 13.5% wheat flour and butter inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CKB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CKB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.02 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $28,000 inventories + $35,000 trade receivables + $8,000 cash = $71,000; 2025 current assets = $22,000 + $48,000 + $15,000 = $85,000. 2024 = $71,000 ÷ $55,000 = 1.29; 2025 = $85,000 ÷ $62,000 = 1.37. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($71,000 − $28,000) ÷ $55,000 = $43,000 ÷ $55,000 = 0.78; 2025 = ($85,000 − $22,000) ÷ $62,000 = $63,000 ÷ $62,000 = 1.02.

Evaluation: CKB's liquidity has clearly improved in quality, not just quantity. The 2025 figures show cash rising from $8,000 to $15,000, giving genuine headroom for the $145,000 wholesale line's early stocking and van repairs. The stock-independent measure crossed the 1.00 threshold — CKB can now pay all current liabilities without selling a single pie — which 2024's 0.78 could not claim. Inventories fell from $28,000 to $22,000 (an efficient 6.1%-waste improvement), reducing write-off risk for fresh pastry. The caveat is trade receivables, which rose from $35,000 to $48,000 as more café accounts bought on weekly credit terms; if those café owners stretch payment, the stronger position could reverse, and current liabilities still rose from $55,000 to $62,000, so discipline is needed on the loan and supplier terms.

Conclusion: CKB's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures strengthened, and critically the improvement survives stripping out inventories, which fell anyway. For a sole trader carrying a new five-year bank loan, this is genuine progress rather than cosmetic stock build-up. The main risk is rising trade receivables, so Rosa should enforce café payment terms and review credit limits while the new wholesale line beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CKB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CKB of installing a computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) proving oven for its pastry line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A CAM-controlled proving oven holds temperature, humidity and timing far more precisely than manual checking, cutting the 2.9% defect rate further and reducing rejected wholesale boxes. Precision baking also lowers the 6.1% flour and butter waste, and automation steadies output on weekend shifts where the 22% labour turnover makes manual quality assurance fragile. Consistent laminated pastry strengthens CKB's reputation for same-day delivery to the 68% of café owners who want it, supporting the new wholesale line and the repayment of the $70,000 bank loan from higher, more reliable margins.

Disadvantage: The CAM oven is a capital commitment on top of the $145,000 wholesale line investment and the $70,000 loan, so CKB takes on heavier fixed capacity and maintenance obligations, including software licences, sensor calibration and specialist repair call-outs that a 12-person sole trader cannot absorb easily. If demand dips in the city region — or café orders grow slower than forecast — the oven's fixed cost per box rises, eroding the $3.75 contribution. Staff also need retraining on the new controls, and any electronic failure during a peak Saturday bake could halt the whole wholesale line until a technician arrives, threatening the same-day delivery promise the range depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CKB's quality, waste, labour turnover and expansion finances.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate cut to 4.5%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in wheat flour and butter costs will affect CKB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate cut (5.0% to 4.5%): For a sole trader carrying a $70,000 five-year bank loan on the new wholesale line, a 0.5% cut saves roughly $350 a year in interest — helpful but small. Lower rates also ease overdraft pressure on the $48,000 trade receivables balance and make any future van purchase (relevant given the ageing fleet) cheaper. The cut genuinely supports small businesses, as the bulletin intends, but its cash benefit to CKB is marginal next to weekly ingredient invoices.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.72 per hour from April 2026): With 12 employees, mainly production and weekend delivery staff, the wage bill rises by about $1,500 a year per full-time worker at the floor rate — roughly $10,000–$18,000 a year across the team, before differentials for skilled pastry staff. For a $90,000 fixed-cost operation this is meaningful, but CKB can partly offset it with the automation of the new line, reduced overtime from better batch planning, and productivity benchmarks (34,000 units ÷ 12 staff ≈ 2,833 boxes per worker).

Input cost inflation (13.5% wheat flour and butter): These two ingredients dominate the $4.75 variable cost per unit. A 13.5% rise adds roughly $0.40–$0.64 per unit; at 34,000 units that is about $13,600–$21,800 a year, direct and unavoidable, hitting every box sold. CKB must either raise prices to its 34 cafés — risking volume — or absorb the hit against the $3.75 contribution, unless the 44% of cafés willing to pay $0.50 more for organic flour can fund the gap.

Conclusion: The 13.5% rise in wheat flour and butter costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit CKB sells, unlike the interest saving which is fixed and small, and unlike the wage rise which can be partially offset by automation and productivity; ingredient inflation is recurring, front-of-mind, and directly reaches cafés' willingness to pay. The wage rise is second; the rate cut is welcome but minor — but CKB must act on all three, renegotiating supplier contracts and pricing the organic premium carefully to protect its $3.75 contribution.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CKB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CKB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CKB with a well-justified judgement that the 13.5% input-cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
